summary:
Yemen's Penal Code 1994 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Article 264 defines homosexuality between men as anal penetration and, for participants who are not married, prescribes 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment; the article prescribes a different penalty where the participants are married. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2026 restates the same provision for events of 2025, and GayLawNet carries the statute as Yemen's canonical criminalisation citation.

The article reaches women as well: Article 268 prescribes up to three years' imprisonment for premeditated lesbianism. A visitor should therefore treat any same-sex conduct, not only conduct between men, as criminal.

Capital exposure is documented, not hypothetical. In January and February 2024, two courts administered by the Houthi authorities in Yemen sentenced more than 40 people to death, flogging or imprisonment over same-sex conduct. The Dhamar criminal court sentenced nine people to death on 23 January 2024, seven by stoning and two by crucifixion, and gave 23 further defendants terms of six months to ten years for homosexuality or spreading immorality; an Ibb court handed additional death sentences on 1 February 2024. Amnesty International called for an immediate halt to the executions and for the release of those facing LGBTI charges. Readings of Article 264 that treat the conduct itself as a capital offence also circulate, and Wikipedia's country coverage records death as the penalty for married men, so a visitor should treat execution as a live risk rather than a remote theoretical maximum.

The statute's territorial reach is contested by the conflict. Cairo 52's country review records that the penal provisions apply only in government-controlled regions, with other parts of the country under competing faction authorities, so legal exposure shifts at front lines and checkpoints. Human Rights Watch makes the same finding for 2025, describing Houthi and government factional control as determining where the law applies.

Formal enforcement is only one layer of exposure. Cairo 52 records that the erosion of the rule of law and growing militia influence mean de-facto criminalisation is rarely enforced by courts in some areas but is used to justify civilians taking matters into their own hands, and IPS's reporting from Sana'a in 2013 describes a gay man hiding his appearance as still problematic in a conservative society with no place for people like him. Discretionary social enforcement thus sits alongside the statutory penalty.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's 2018 report Audacity in Adversity places Yemen among 14 countries in the Middle East and North Africa where zina provisions criminalise sex outside marriage and same-sex acts are explicitly prohibited, and notes the use of breach of modesty laws against expression. The report could identify no activists in Yemen willing to speak about their work, a documented safety gap that removes a routine avenue through which a visitor might otherwise seek local contact or current ground information.

The country's wider instability conditions how protection machinery functions. Human Rights Watch describes the humanitarian crisis as among the world's worst, with 19.5 million people needing aid, alongside the factional control that determines which courts and which penal provisions reach a given area. Cairo 52 pairs that crisis with erosion of the rule of law and expanding militia influence as the background against which de-facto criminalisation operates.

The same-sex conduct charges have been pursued under the auspices of religious justification as well as statute, and the Dhamar and Ibb sentences show that courts outside the capital's reach continue to impose the most severe penalties available to them.
localsOnly:
The Constitution of the Republic of Yemen, as amended in 2001, does not address LGBTQ rights explicitly. It guarantees certain human rights to all citizens only on the condition that all legislation be compatible with Islamic Shariah law, which leaves same-sex conduct and gender non-conformity without constitutional standing.

The state provides no protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Article 268 of the Penal Code applies specifically to women, prescribing up to three years' imprisonment for premeditated lesbianism, so lesbian and bisexual women face a distinct statutory charge rather than only the male-centred terms of Article 264.

Residents in Sana'a describe concealment as a condition of ordinary life, including hiding long hair under a hood, in a society described as having no place for gay people. Court sentences in 2024, including those from the Houthi-administered courts, were publicly used to signal moral enforcement, and the penalty structure applies to citizens as fully as to visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty structure where the participants are married is not resolved across the sources. Article 264 as carried by GayLawNet and Human Rights Watch states 100 lashes and up to one year for unmarried participants and indicates only that the article prescribes differently for married participants; Wikipedia states death for married men, and current readings treating the conduct as a capital offence circulate without a cited statutory clause confirming that this is codified rather than applied. Whether the capital penalty derives from the statute, from Shariah application, or from discretionary sentencing in Houthi-administered courts is not sourced here.

No source in this inventory addresses entry and visa rules, passport gender markers, airport or border screening that could disclose a visitor's status, access to healthcare or gender-affirming care, facilities or bathroom rules, hate-crime provisions, or partner and marriage recognition. Those fields remain unsourced for Yemen rather than negative findings.

The practical scope of the Penal Code after February 2024 is unclear: the inventory documents sentences from two Houthi-run courts in January and February 2024 but does not record whether those death sentences were carried out, nor the enforcement position of government-controlled courts during the same period.
